h1: Gateway beer styles for friends new to craft beer
title: Gateway Beer Styles for New Drinkers | Craft Beer School
desc: Which craft beer styles to order for friends who only drink mass market lager, how to build a first flight and what to avoid on the first visit.
teaser: Your friend drinks only strong lager and you want to take them to a brewpub. Start here, not with a triple IPA.
standfirst: Introducing a friend to craft beer goes best when you start close to what they already like and move one step at a time. Here are the styles that work as a first step and how to order them.
sections: Start from what they already drink

Most new craft drinkers in India come from mass market lager: very cold, light or strong, crisp and with little bitterness. Their palate is used to that. If you hand them a 70 IBU IPA or a sour fruit beer first, they may decide craft beer is not for them.

The trick is to move one step at a time. Start with something familiar but better made, then add one new flavour at a time: fruit and spice, then hops, then roast. Ask what they like in food and drink too. Someone who enjoys black coffee may love a stout. Someone who likes fresh lime soda may enjoy a wheat beer or a gentle sour.
Step one: clean lagers and kölsch

Start with a helles, pilsner or kölsch. These are pale, crisp and clean, like the lager they know, but with more malt flavour and a fresher finish. A good pilsner shows how much flavour a simple beer can carry. It is a gentle introduction to the idea that beer can taste of bread, honey or herbs.

If they enjoy the pilsner but find it a little bitter, a helles or kölsch is softer.

Wheat beers are the most reliable gateway in India. A hefeweizen has banana and clove from yeast, a soft body and plenty of fizz. A witbier has orange peel and coriander, light and refreshing. Neither is very bitter, both are easy to like and both suit hot weather and Indian food. Our hefeweizen guide covers the German style in detail.

Many people who say they do not like beer enjoy a witbier. The citrus and spice feel familiar.
Step three: gentle hops and amber

Once they are comfortable, try an amber ale or Vienna lager for caramel and toast, or a session IPA or pale ale for hop aroma without heavy bitterness. The point is to introduce hop flavour gradually. Mango, citrus or pine aroma can be a revelation if bitterness does not overwhelm it.

Fruit beers can also work at this step, especially those made with real fruit such as mango, jamun or passion fruit. Avoid very sweet or artificially flavoured versions, which can give the wrong impression.

Dark beer scares some people because they expect it to be heavy or bitter. A milk stout or oatmeal stout is smooth and slightly sweet, tasting of chocolate and coffee. It changes minds quickly. A porter is another good option: roasty but not harsh.

Save very strong or very bitter beers, such as imperial stout, double IPA or barleywine, for later visits.

A flight of four small glasses, usually 90 to 150 ml each, is the best way to explore. Our beer flight guide explains how to order and taste one. For a first visit, try this order:

  1. Pilsner or helles
  2. Witbier or hefeweizen
  3. Amber ale or session IPA
  4. Milk stout or porter

Taste from light to dark and from low to high bitterness. Ask your friend to pick a favourite and then order a full glass of that one. Our guide to reading a taproom menu helps decode ABV, IBU and style names on the board.
What to avoid on a first visit

Skip anything above about 7% ABV, very bitter IPAs, intense sours and heavily smoked beers on the first trip. They are great beers but challenging introductions. Also avoid ordering for your friend without asking. Let them read the board, taste samples if the taproom offers them and choose. A beer they picked themselves is more likely to win them over than one you insisted on.

Order food. Beer is easier to enjoy with snacks. Pairings also help new drinkers understand flavour. Keep pours small and the pace slow. Make sure there is water on the table and that nobody drives home after drinking. If a friend does not drink alcohol, many taprooms offer non alcoholic beer, kombucha or soft drinks so they can still join in.

Most of all, ask questions rather than lecturing. What do they taste? Do they like it? Why? The goal is curiosity, not converting anyone. Over time, the person who started with lager may become the one recommending beers to you.

The hardest part of introducing beer is describing what you taste so the other person understands. Words like malty, hoppy or roasty mean different things to different people. Learning a shared vocabulary for aroma and flavour makes those conversations easier and makes your recommendations more useful.
faqs: What is the best first craft beer for a lager drinker?
A pilsner, helles or kölsch. They are crisp and familiar but show more flavour than mass market lager.
Is wheat beer good for beginners?
Yes. Hefeweizen and witbier are low in bitterness, fruity and refreshing, which makes them a reliable gateway.
Should I start a friend on IPA?
Usually not. High bitterness can put new drinkers off. Try a session IPA or pale ale after they have enjoyed lighter styles.
